title: HTTP for Frontend Engineers
summary: The slice of HTTP a frontend engineer actually touches day to day: methods and idempotency, error-path status codes, and the caching headers that decide whether fetch returns fresh data or a stale surprise.

slides.markdown:
Frontend engineers don't need the full HTTP spec — `computer-networks` owns the protocol mechanics. What actually shows up in your code is narrower: which method to use and whether it's safe to retry, which status codes your `fetch` error handling needs to branch on, which headers you read or set, and — the one that causes the most real bugs — **caching**.

A `fetch` returning a `200` doesn't mean fresh data. It might mean the browser handed you a year-old cached response without touching the network at all. Getting caching semantics wrong produces some of the hardest-to-reproduce bugs in frontend work, because they depend on cache state the developer can't see just by reading the code.

This topic covers the HTTP surface you'll actually write against, ending with the caching model in enough depth to debug it in production.

Every request you send has a **method**, a **URL**, **headers**, and optionally a **body**. Every response has a **status code**, **headers**, and a **body**. That's the whole shape — the rest of HTTP is conventions layered on top of it.

As a frontend engineer, you write against this shape constantly without necessarily naming it: `fetch(url, { method, headers, body })` is literally constructing a request; `response.status`, `response.headers.get(...)`, and `await response.json()` are reading the response's three parts back out.

One detail worth internalizing early: headers are **case-insensitive** by spec but conventionally written in a consistent casing, and `fetch`'s `Headers` object normalizes lookups for you — `headers.get('content-type')` and `headers.get('Content-Type')` return the same thing.

The methods you'll actually use, and the property that matters most about each: **idempotency** — can you safely retry the same request without changing the outcome beyond the first call?

- **GET** — idempotent, safe to retry, safe to cache.
- **PUT** — idempotent by design: "set this resource to exactly this value" gives the same end state whether sent once or five times.
- **DELETE** — idempotent: deleting an already-deleted resource is a no-op (though the status code on the retry may differ, e.g. `404` instead of `204`).
- **POST** — **not** idempotent. "Create a new order" run twice creates two orders. This is why retrying a failed POST automatically is dangerous without an idempotency key.
- **PATCH** — **not guaranteed** idempotent, depends on the patch semantics — `{"balance": 100}` is idempotent, `{"balance_delta": +10}` is not.

This is the property that decides whether your retry logic, or a browser's automatic retry on a flaky connection, is safe to apply blindly.

slides.sectionTitle: Status codes your error handling actually branches on
slides.markdown:
`fetch` only rejects its promise on a **network failure** — a `404` or `500` is still a "successful" fetch as far as the promise is concerned, with `response.ok === false`. This trips up nearly everyone new to `fetch` coming from libraries that throw on any non-2xx.

The codes worth branching on explicitly:

- **401** — not authenticated; typically triggers a redirect to login or a token refresh attempt.
- **403** — authenticated but not authorized; a different UI state than 401 (don't send someone to a login screen when logging in again won't fix it).
- **404** — resource doesn't exist; distinct from a network failure.
- **429** — rate limited; often comes with a `Retry-After` header your retry logic should honor.
- **5xx** — server-side failure; usually the case where a generic retry-with-backoff is appropriate, unlike 4xx codes which usually mean retrying identically won't help.

Treating all non-2xx responses as one generic "error" state is the most common miss here — 401 and 404 need genuinely different UI responses.

A short list covers most day-to-day frontend HTTP work:

- **`Content-Type`** — you set it on requests (`application/json`, `multipart/form-data` for uploads) and read it on responses to know how to parse the body.
- **`Authorization`** — carries a bearer token or similar credential; you set this, the browser never adds it automatically the way it does with cookies.
- **`Accept`** — tells the server what response format you can handle; `fetch` sets a permissive default, but APIs with content negotiation (returning JSON vs XML) read this.

The asymmetry between `Authorization` and cookies matters for security design: cookies ride along on every request to their origin automatically (which is what makes them CSRF-able); an `Authorization` header is only sent when your code explicitly attaches it, which is one reason token-based auth and cookie-based auth have different threat models — covered further in `cookies-and-web-storage`.

Three headers decide what the browser does the *next* time it needs the same URL, and knowing them precisely is the core skill of this topic:

- **`Cache-Control: max-age=N`** — cache this for N seconds and treat it as fresh; no network request at all until it expires. `no-cache` (confusingly) means "always revalidate," not "don't cache." `no-store` means genuinely never cache it.
- **`ETag`** — an opaque version identifier for the response body. On the next request past `max-age`, the browser sends `If-None-Match: <etag>`; the server replies `304 Not Modified` (no body) if it still matches, or `200` with a new body and new ETag if it changed.
- **`Last-Modified`** — the older, coarser cousin of ETag: a timestamp, checked via `If-Modified-Since`, revalidated the same way but at second-level granularity instead of exact content matching.

The three states that matter are **fresh** (serve from cache, no request), **stale-but-revalidatable** (send a conditional request, maybe get a cheap 304), and **miss** (no cached copy, full request).

Every request to a previously-fetched URL walks the same decision: is there a cached response? Is it still within `max-age`? If yes, serve it, zero network round trips. If it's past `max-age` but has a validator (`ETag`/`Last-Modified`), send a conditional request — a `304` means "still good, reset the freshness clock," a `200` means "here's new content, cache it." If there's no cached copy at all, it's a full miss and a normal request happens.

slides.markdown:
Beyond what the HTTP cache does automatically, application code often layers its own strategy on top, and the two ends of the spectrum fit different data:

| Strategy | Behavior | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Cache-first** | Serve cached data immediately if present; only fetch if absent or explicitly invalidated | App shell assets, rarely-changing config, static images |
| **Network-first** | Always attempt a fresh fetch; fall back to cache only on failure | Live data — prices, inventory, a chat feed |

The wrong choice in either direction has a concrete cost: cache-first on a live price feed shows stale prices as if they were current; network-first on your app's static JS bundle adds a needless round trip on every load for content that never changes. Picking per-resource-type, not globally, is what a real caching strategy looks like — covered further for offline scenarios in `service-workers-and-offline`.

slides.sectionTitle: fetch with cache control and timeouts
A cached 200 is not a fresh 200
slides.markdown:
The trap: `response.status === 200` tells you the request succeeded, not that the data is current. A `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` response served on request #47 within that hour is still a `200` — from the cache, with no network activity at all, potentially showing data that's been stale for 59 minutes.

This produces a specific, hard-to-reproduce bug pattern: "I updated the data on the server, but the app still shows the old value" — the fix isn't in your application code, it's in the response's caching headers not matching how fresh the data actually needs to be. Debugging it means checking the Network tab's **Size** column (it says "(disk cache)" or "(memory cache)" instead of a byte count when served from cache) — status code alone won't tell you.

For genuinely live data, either the server needs to send `no-cache` (forcing revalidation every time) or the client needs to bypass the cache explicitly with `cache: 'no-store'`.

Idempotency (from earlier) is what makes automatic retry logic safe or dangerous. A network layer that blindly retries on timeout is fine for a `GET` — retrying doesn't change anything. Blindly retrying a `POST` for "create an order" on a timeout can create a **duplicate order**, because you genuinely don't know if the first request succeeded server-side before the response was lost.

The production-grade fix is an **idempotency key**: the client generates a unique key per logical operation (a UUID), sends it as a header, and the server deduplicates — if it sees the same key twice, it returns the result of the first attempt instead of executing again. Stripe's payments API popularized this pattern precisely because retrying a payment request safely is a genuine business requirement, not a nice-to-have.

As a rule: retry GET/PUT/DELETE freely; never retry a bare POST without either an idempotency key or explicit confirmation that the original request never reached the server.
